question: Which three limits decide the maximum landing mass of a Class A aeroplane?

options.text: Tyre speed, brake energy and structural limits on the day
Field length, cost index and fuel limits

explanation: The maximum landing mass is the lowest of the landing climb limit, the field length limit and the maximum structural landing mass.

question: What all-engines landing climb gradient is required of a Class A aeroplane?
explanation: With all engines in the landing configuration, the steady climb gradient must be at least 3.2%.

question: For the all-engines landing climb requirement, what thrust is assumed?

options.text: Take-off thrust available immediately as the levers move
Maximum continuous thrust on all engines

explanation: The thrust is that available 8 seconds after starting to move the thrust levers from minimum flight idle to the take-off position.

question: At what speed and configuration is the all-engines landing climb gradient demonstrated?
explanation: The landing climb (baulked landing) is demonstrated in the landing configuration at VREF.

question: What one-engine-inoperative discontinued approach gradient is required of a twin-engine Class A aeroplane?
explanation: The approach climb requires 2.1% for twins, 2.4% for three engines and 2.7% for four.

question: What discontinued approach gradient is required of a four-engine Class A aeroplane?
explanation: Four-engine aeroplanes need at least 2.7% with one engine inoperative in the approach configuration.

question: In what configuration is the one-engine-inoperative approach climb demonstrated?

options.text: Gear up, approach flap, remaining engines at go-around thrust
Gear down, approach flap, remaining engines at idle
Gear up, flaps up, remaining engines at MCT
Gear down, landing flap, all engines at go-around thrust

explanation: The critical engine is inoperative, the others at go-around thrust, with the gear retracted and flaps at the approach setting.

question: For the approach climb, what condition applies to the approach flap setting?

options.text: It must be the take-off flap setting
Its VSR must not exceed 110% of the landing flap VSR
It must be the fully retracted setting
It must give a reference stall speed below the landing flap VSR

explanation: Approach flaps may be used provided their reference stall speed does not exceed 110% of the landing flap VSR.

question: What is the maximum speed for the approach climb demonstration?
explanation: The approach climb speed is the normal approach speed, but not greater than 1.4 VSR.

question: How is the landing climb limit mass found from the two climb requirements?

options.text: Only the all-engines landing climb requirement is used

explanation: The more limiting of the landing and approach climb requirements gives the maximum mass for altitude and temperature (the landing WAT limit).

question: For an instrument approach with a decision height below 200 ft, what missed approach gradient must be available with one engine inoperative?

options.text: 2.5%, or the published value if higher
At least 2.1%, or the published gradient if that is less

explanation: The approach mass must allow a one-engine-inoperative missed approach gradient of at least 2.5%, or the published gradient if that is greater.

question: What is the dry landing distance requirement for a turbojet aeroplane?

options.text: A full stop from 50 ft within 70% of the LDA
A full stop from 50 ft within 85% of the LDA
A full stop from 35 ft within 60% of the LDA
A full stop from 50 ft within 60% of the LDA

explanation: Turbojets must land and stop from 50 ft within 60% of the LDA at destination and alternates.

question: What is the dry landing distance requirement for a turboprop aeroplane?
explanation: Turboprops must stop within 70% of the LDA. The extra allowance reflects their more effective propeller reverse thrust.

question: Which factor converts a jet's dry landing distance into the required LDA?
explanation: 1 ÷ 0.6 ≈ 1.67 for jets; 1 ÷ 0.7 ≈ 1.43 for turboprops.

question: A jet's dry landing distance from 50 ft is 1 500 m. What is the minimum LDA?
explanation: 1 500 ÷ 0.6 = 2 500 m. Using the turboprop factor (÷ 0.7) gives about 2 143 m.

question: A runway has an LDA of 2 400 m. What is the greatest dry landing distance allowed for a jet?
explanation: 60% of 2 400 = 1 440 m. 1 680 m is the turboprop (70%) value.

question: A turboprop's dry landing distance is 1 400 m. What is the minimum LDA?
explanation: 1 400 ÷ 0.7 = 2 000 m. Using the jet factor gives 2 333 m.

question: What is required if the runway may be wet at the estimated time of arrival?

options.text: The dry landing distance is multiplied by 1.43
The LDA must be at least 150% of the dry required distance
The LDA must be at least 115% of the dry required distance
No extra margin is needed for wet runways

explanation: For a wet runway the LDA must be at least 115% of the required dry landing distance, unless an approved lower factor is published in the flight manual.

question: A jet needs an LDA of 2 500 m on a dry runway. What LDA is needed if the runway may be wet?
When may short landing or steep approach procedures be approved?

options.text: With screen heights as low as 15 ft on long runways
Only with a 50 ft screen height

explanation: Approved short landing and steep approach procedures may use lower screen heights, but not less than 35 ft.

question: Which temperature is used in the Class A landing distance calculation?

options.text: The highest temperature of the day

explanation: The landing distance is based on aerodrome pressure altitude and standard day (ISA) temperature, with factored winds and slope where it exceeds ±2%.

question: When is runway slope accounted for in the Class A landing distance?

options.text: Only for downslopes of more than 1%

explanation: The landing distance accounts for runway slope if it is greater than ±2%.

question: What speed at 50 ft is assumed for the Class A landing distance?
explanation: The landing distance is based on a 50 ft speed of not less than 1.23 VSR0 (and not less than VMCL).

question: What is VMCL?

options.text: The approach control speed with an engine out
The air control speed after take-off
The minimum landing speed with all engines at idle and full flap
The ground control speed after an engine failure

explanation: VMCL is the CAS at which, with the critical engine suddenly inoperative on the approach, control can be maintained in straight flight with no more than 5° bank towards the live engine(s).

question: Which other requirement must VREF meet besides the speed margins?

options.text: It must be below VMO by at least 100 kt in all configurations

explanation: VREF must be no less than VMCL and 1.23 VSR0, and must give the manoeuvring capability specified in the certification rules.

question: Which two cases must be checked for landing at the destination?

options.text: Best runway still air; likely runway forecast wind
The longest runway, and the runway nearest the terminal building

explanation: The landing must be checked both on the most favourable runway in still air and on the runway most likely to be used in the forecast wind; the lower mass is used.

question: An aerodrome has a single runway and the still-air requirement cannot be met, so a landing needs some headwind. When may the aeroplane be despatched?

options.text: If the commander accepts the risk and signs the load sheet

explanation: If the still-air case cannot be met at a single-runway aerodrome, the aeroplane may be despatched only with two alternates at which full compliance is possible.

question: The forecast-wind requirement cannot be met at the destination. When may the aeroplane be despatched?

options.text: If the landing mass is increased to improve braking on arrival

explanation: If the forecast-wind case cannot be met, an alternate at which all the landing requirements are met must be designated.

question: Still air allows 64 000 kg; the forecast wind on the likely runway allows 66 500 kg; the structural limit is 65 000 kg. What is the limiting landing mass for the field lengths?
explanation: The lower of the still-air and forecast-wind masses is used, 64 000 kg, which is also below the structural limit.

question: How may a landing distance graph be used?

options.text: Only to find the approach speed
Only to find a landing distance for a given mass, never the reverse

explanation: Landing graphs are used in the normal direction (mass to distance) and in reverse (distance available to maximum mass).

question: Why are turboprops given a less demanding landing factor than jets?

options.text: Reverse is quicker and lasts longer

explanation: Propeller reverse can be selected quickly and used down to a stop, while jet reverse takes time to deploy and must be cancelled at low speed.
